rows.text: One family, three personalities, one cause. **HCl** (bond 431 kJ/mol) is stable, the weakest reducer, and the only one clean enough to make with oxidising H₂SO₄; **HBr** (366) needs H₃PO₄ because H₂SO₄ turns half its bromide into brown Br₂; **HI** (299) is so reducing it reduces the sulphate to SO₂ while turning to violet I₂ vapour.…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "Thermal stability of the hydrogen halides decreases from HCl to HI, while their reducing power and acidic strength increase."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The self-defeating preparation*** — try to make HI with concentrated H2SO4 and the acid oxidises its own product: the iodide reduces the sulphate to SO2 while becoming brown I2 vapour. H3PO4, too weak to oxidise anything, is the only honest choice.

rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — One Family, Three Personalities HCl, HBr and HI: same formula shape, steeply different behaviour. This topic compares their preparation, properties, reducing strength, acidic nature and solubility — and explains every trend from the bond.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Preparation - **HCl (lab):** NaCl + conc. H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl (below 200 °C; dry gas, upward delivery — heavier than air). Industrial: burning H₂ in Cl₂ (synthesis), or by-product of chlorination. - **HBr:** cannot use conc. H₂SO₄ (it oxidises Br⁻ to Br₂); use **KBr + conc. rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: H2SO4 only for HCl; H3PO4 for HBr/HI. Stability: HCl > HBr > HI. Reducing: HI > HBr > HCl. Acid: HI strongest. Proof: 2HI + H2SO4 -> I2 + SO2 + 2H2O. AgX: white/cream/yellow.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): How is hydrogen chloride prepared in the laboratory? Why is the same method not used for HI?** — **HCl:** dry sodium chloride is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid below 200 °C: **NaCl + H₂SO₄(conc) → NaHSO₄ + HCl**. The gas is dried with concentrated H₂SO₄ and collected by **upward delivery** (heavier than air).…  ·  **NEB-style (2m): Arrange HCl, HBr and HI in order of (a) thermal stability and (b) reducing strength, with reasons.** — **(a) Stability: HCl > HBr > HI.** Bond energies fall 431 → 366 → 299 kJ/mol as the bond lengthens (127 → 141 → 161 pm); the weaker the bond, the more easily heat snaps it, so HI decomposes visibly (2HI → H₂ + I₂)…

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: One weak bond explains three trends: as H-X lengthens down the group the bond both releases its proton more easily (acidity up) and snaps homolytically more easily (stability down, reducing power up) — HI is the strongest acid AND the strongest reducer of the three.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: HCl/HBr/HHI comparative study. Prep: HCl from NaCl + conc H2SO4 (< 200 C, upward delivery); HBr and HI need NON-oxidising conc H3PO4 (KBr/KI + H3PO4) because conc H2SO4 oxidises Br- to Br2 and I- to I2 (2HI + H2SO4 -> I2 + SO2 + 2H2O).…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Your stomach makes roughly 2 litres of 0.1 M HCl every day — the same molecule that pickles steel digests your lunch.

rows.text: ## 3. Scientific Definitions | Term | Scientific meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | **Hydrogen halide** | Binary compound of H and a halogen | HCl, HBr, HI | | **Reducing strength** | Ease of halide ion oxidation | I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ | | **Thermal stability** | Resistance to decomposition by heat | HCl > HBr > HI | | **Fuming** | White acidic mist in moist air | all three HX | |…  ·  ## 4. Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Why H₂SO₄ is disqualified for HBr and HI - Concentrated H₂SO₄ is an oxidising acid. With NaCl it merely forms HCl (Cl⁻ too weak a reducer to be oxidised further). With KBr it oxidises half the bromide to Br₂ (2KBr + 2H₂SO₄(conc) → K₂SO₄ + Br₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O) — the gas comes out contaminated and purple.…  ·  ## 5.
